title: Asking for directions
goal: Ask the way, understand directions, and use both informal and polite commands.
bekal: asking the way to a place
asking someone to repeat when you miss it

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En la calle
dialogs.intro: Asking a police officer. Every verb she uses is a polite command.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Siga todo recto hasta la plaza.
lines.id: Keep going straight until the square.
lines.literal: continue(formal) all straight until the square.

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Gire a la derecha y tome la segunda calle.
lines.id: Turn right and take the second street.
lines.literal: turn(formal) to-the right and take(formal) the second street.

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Exacto. Cruce el semáforo y siga cien metros.
lines.id: Exactly. Cross at the traffic lights and carry on for a hundred meters.
lines.literal: exact. cross(formal) the traffic-light and continue(formal) one-hundred meters.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Is it very far? I'm in a hurry.

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Diez minutos a pie. También puede tomar el autobús número cinco.
lines.id: Ten minutes on foot. You can also take the number five bus.
lines.literal: ten minutes on foot. also you(formal)-can take the bus number five.

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Enfrente del banco. No tiene pérdida.
lines.id: In front of the bank. You can't miss it.
lines.literal: in-front of-the bank. not you(formal)-have loss.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Muchas gracias. ¿Me lo repite, por favor?
lines.id: Thank you very much. Could you repeat that, please?

lines.speaker: Policía:
lines.text: Claro. Todo recto, segunda a la derecha, y está allí.
lines.id: Of course. Straight on, second on the right, and you're there.
lines.literal: of-course. all straight, second to the right, and it-is-located there.

notes: **Polite commands are formed by swapping the vowel.** Take the present *yo* form, drop the -o, and add the **opposite** vowel: -ar verbs get **-e** (*girar → gire*), -er/-ir verbs get **-a** (*comer → coma*, *seguir → siga*). This swap — not an extra word — is what makes the sentence sound formal.

**With friends, the form is actually simpler:** exactly the same as the "he/she" form. *Sigue todo recto*, *gira a la derecha*, *toma el autobús*. So *gire* for someone you call *usted*, *gira* for someone you call *tú*.

**Ordinals: primero, segundo, tercero, cuarto, quinto.** Two of them shorten before a masculine singular noun: *el primer día*, *el tercer piso* — but stay whole for feminine ones: *la primera calle*.

**Many physical states use tener where English uses "be".** *Tengo prisa* (I'm in a hurry), *tengo hambre* (I'm hungry), *tengo sed* (I'm thirsty), *tengo frío* (I'm cold), *tengo sueño* (I'm sleepy). You "have" them all, just like age in Unit 7.
**Coger or tomar?** In Spain *coger el autobús* is completely normal. In most of Latin America the word is vulgar, so people say *tomar* or *agarrar*. When in doubt, *tomar* is safe everywhere.
**Exacto, eso es, correcto** — three ways to tell someone they're right. The one you'll hear most is *exacto*, said briskly.
**No tiene pérdida** literally "you have no loss", meaning "you can't miss it". You'll hear it every time you ask the way in Spain.
**The lifesaver: ¿Me lo repite, por favor?** Never be shy about using it. Two others just as important: *¿Puede hablar más despacio?* and *No entiendo, lo siento.*

grammars.title: Commands
body: Compare the two columns below. The informal one (*tú*) keeps the original vowel; the polite one (*usted*) swaps it. To say "don't", just add *no* to the polite form: *No gire aquí*.
after: Eight verbs have completely irregular informal commands, and all are very common: *decir → di*, *hacer → haz*, *ir → ve*, *poner → pon*, *salir → sal*, *ser → sé*, *tener → ten*, *venir → ven*. Their polite forms are regular again: *diga, haga, vaya, ponga, salga, sea, tenga, venga*.

Saying "don't" with *tú* doesn't use the informal command, but the polite form plus -s: *no gires*, *no tomes*, *no vayas*. That's why *ven* (come) turns into *no vengas* (don't come) — two words that look nothing alike.

blocks.text: You don't need to be able to say all of these — just recognize them when someone in a hurry rattles them off.

head: Español
Meaning
rows: Tome la primera calle a la derecha.
Take the first street on the right.
Está al final de la calle.
It's at the end of the street.
Lo siento, no soy de aquí.
Sorry, I'm not from around here.

blocks.title: If you didn't catch it
items: *¿Puede hablar más despacio, por favor?* — Could you speak more slowly?
*¿Me lo repite, por favor?* — Could you repeat that?
*¿Cómo se dice … en español?* — How do you say … in Spanish?
*No entiendo. Soy extranjero.* — I don't understand. I'm a foreigner.
*¿Me lo puede escribir?* — Could you write it down? This one saves you most: writing can't be spoken too fast.

exercises.prompt: Complete with the right direction word.
items: El banco está en la ____ de la calle Mayor.
La farmacia está a la ____, al lado del café.
El museo está al ____ de esta calle.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Spanish (use the polite form).
items: Excuse me, where's the bus stop?
Turn left at the traffic lights.
I'm in a hurry, is the station far?

answers: gire a la izquierda — tome el autobús — siga todo recto — cruce la plaza — suba las escaleras — pase el semáforo

Perdone, ¿dónde está la parada? — Gire a la izquierda en el semáforo. — Tome la tercera calle. — Tengo prisa, ¿está lejos la estación? — ¿Puede hablar más despacio? — Un billete de ida y vuelta para Sevilla.
